Critical gate distance for Wigner crystallization in the two-dimensional electron gas

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Agnes Valenti Thanks: A.V. and V.C. contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, NY, 10010, USA    Vladimir Calvera Thanks: A.V. and V.C. contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Department of Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of California, Santa Barbara, California 93106, USA    Yubo Yang Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, NY, 10010, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, Hofstra University, Hempstead, New York 11549, USA    Miguel A. Morales Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, NY, 10010, USA    Steven A. Kivelson Affiliation: Department of Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA    Ilya Esterlis Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, USA    Shiwei Zhang Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, NY, 10010, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We report on the properties of the two-dimensional electron gas in a dual-gate geometry, using quantum Monte Carlo methods to obtain aspects of the phase diagram as a function of electron density and gate distance. We identify the critical gate distance below which the Wigner crystal phase disappears. For larger gate distances, the system undergoes a re-entrant transition from crystal to liquid at sufficiently low density. We also present preliminary evidence for a fully polarized ferromagnetic liquid state at low electron density and intermediate gate distances. The quantum Monte Carlo results are compared with simpler approximate methods, which are shown to be semi-quantitatively reliable for determining key features of the phase diagram. These methods are then used to obtain the phase boundary between the Wigner crystal and liquid in the single-gate geometry.

Introduction. The two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) plays a central role in the study of strongly correlated electronic systems, largely due to its simplicity and the rich phenomena it exhibits. As a function of increasing density nn, the 2DEG can be tuned from a solid phase at small nn – the Wigner crystal (WC) – to a strongly correlated liquid and ultimately to a weakly interacting Fermi gas at large nn. While the detailed nature of the zero-temperature phase diagram as a function of nn remains a subject of active investigation [1, 2, 3, *Waintal2006_hybrid, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], many salient properties of the 2DEG are now quantitatively well understood, thanks primarily to quantum Monte Carlo methods [11, 12, 13, 8].

In most experimental setups, the 2DEG is created near metallic gate electrodes, separated by a distance dd from the electron layer 11 1 For a given experimental system, the value of dd may have to be rescaled d→ϵ∥/ϵ⟂×dd\to\sqrt{\epsilon_{\parallel}/\epsilon_{\perp}}\times d to properly account for an anisotropic dielectric constant of the 2DEG environment; e.g., as in hBN [14].. The effects of the gate on the properties of the electronic system become significant when dd is smaller than the average inter-electron distance rsr_{s} (measured in units of the Bohr radius aBa_{B}), at which point gate screening renders the Coulomb interactions effectively short-ranged. As an additional tuning parameter in the phase diagram of the 2DEG, the gate distance dd influences the competition between the electron liquid and WC phases – causing the WC phase to disappear entirely for sufficiently small dd [1] – and may even stabilize new phases not present in the pure Coulomb problem.

In the present paper, we use Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) to investigate the effects of symmetric gate electrodes on the properties of the clean 2DEG. We focus on the liquid and WC phases, and map out the liquid-solid phase diagram in the (rs,d)(r_{s},d)-plane. In particular, we identify the critical gate distance dcd_{c} for the existence of a WC phase in the dual-gated geometry. We also provide preliminary evidence for the existence of a narrow region of ferromagnetic liquid at low density and finite dd. Our primary results are summarized in the phase diagram in Fig. 1.

We also highlight some approximate methods for determining ground-state energies and the liquid/solid phase boundary that we have found to be in semi-quantitative agreement with the more accurate DMC calculations. The reliability of these approximate methods suggests a simple route by which to make estimates for the more structured 2DEGs realized in different materials and devices. As an additional example, we analyze the single gate system using these methods.

Screened two-dimensional electron gas. We consider a 2DEG with interactions screened by two symmetric, parallel metal gates, each at a distance dd from the 2DEG (see Fig. 1). The Hamiltonian is given by

H=−∑i12∇i2+∑i<jVsc(|𝐫i−𝐫j|)+b.g..\displaystyle H=-\sum\limits_{i}\frac{1}{2}{\bf\nabla}_{i}^{2}+\sum\limits_{i<j}V_{\rm sc}(|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}|)+\text{b.g.}. (1)

Labels i,ji,j run over all electrons, VscV_{\rm sc} is the dual-gate screened potential, and “b.g.” represents the neutralizing background. Throughout this work we measure lengths in units of the Bohr radius aB=4​π​ϵ0​ℏ2/m​e2a_{\text{B}}=4\pi\epsilon_{0}\hbar^{2}/me^{2} and energies in Hartree Ha=ℏ2/m​aB2{\rm Ha}=\hbar^{2}/ma_{\text{B}}^{2}.

The phase diagram of the dual-gated system is determined by the gate distance dd and the Wigner-Seitz radius rs=1/π​nr_{s}=1/\sqrt{\pi n}, where nn is the electron density. On the one hand, the strength of the interaction is controlled by rsr_{s}: The ratio between (classical) potential and kinetic energy is roughly measured by rsr_{s}. On the other hand, the range of the interactions is controlled by the gate distance dd: The metal gates screen the interactions which results in strong suppression at distances larger than dd. The gate-screened interaction is given by

Vsc​(|𝐫i−𝐫j|)\displaystyle V_{\rm sc}(|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}|) =1(2​π)2​∫d​𝐪​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​vsc​(𝐪),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int{\rm d}{\bf q}\,{\rm e}^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j})}v_{\rm sc}({\bf q}), (2)
vsc​(𝐪)\displaystyle v_{\rm sc}({\bf q}) =e22​ϵ0​tanh⁡(d​|𝐪|)|𝐪|,\displaystyle=\frac{e^{2}}{2\epsilon_{0}}\frac{\tanh(d|{\bf q}|)}{|{\bf q}|}, (3)

with limiting behavior Vsc(r)∼e−πr/2dV_{\rm sc}(r)\sim{\rm e}^{-\pi r/2d} for r≫dr\gg d [15].

DMC approach. DMC constitutes one of the most accurate methods for the study of strongly correlated systems such as the electron gas [16, 17, 13, 12, 18], achieving quantitative agreement with experiments while having no tunable parameters [19, 9]. Within DMC, an ensemble of electron configurations is evolved in imaginary time towards the ground state. Fermionic symmetry is ensured by employing the fixed-node (phase) approximation. Here, the nodal structure is fixed by a trial wave-function, with parameters optimized by a variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculation for each system (rsr_{s}, dd, number of electrons, and boundary condition). Here, we utilize trial wave-functions of the Slater-Jastrow and Slater-Jastrow-Backflow type [20, 21, 22, 23, 24] within the package QMCPACK [25, 26], with appropriate modifications. The orbitals in the Slater determinant are evaluated at quasiparticle coordinates if backflow transformations are employed (which we only use for fluid trial wave-functions). The Jastrow factor and backflow transformation are parametrized using polynomial bsplines [25].

As a result of the fixed-node (phase) approximation, the choice of orbitals reflects the physical phase of the system. Capitalizing on the variational nature of DMC, we study the phase diagram of the screened 2DEG by comparing energies obtained with different physical choices of single-particle orbitals. Here we consider both fluid and crystalline trial states of varying polarization. For the Fermi fluid, we utilize plane wave orbitals exp⁡(i​𝐤⋅𝐫)\exp(i{\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}) to construct paramagnetic and ferromagnetic fluid trial wave-functions. For the crystalline states, we use Gaussian orbitals of the form exp⁡(−C​r2)\exp(-Cr^{2}), localized on the sites of the triangular WC lattice, with width controlled by the variational parameter CC. We consider only the antiferromagnetic (with alternating lines of spin-up and spin-down electrons) and ferromagnetic crystals, based on results in the unscreened 2DEG [13, 8]22 2 We note that more complex anti-ferromagnetic orders have not been ruled out [27, *misguich1999, 29].. All simulations are performed with N=56N=56 electrons (and N=120N=120 in special cases). Finite-size effects are reduced by performing twist-averaging using 2525 quasi-random twists for all liquid wave-functions [30], chosen from the low-discrepancy Halton sequence [31]. Many-body finite-size effects due to the interaction remain [32, 33], but are expected to be small, especially as the Coulomb potential is screened.

Extrapolated estimates. We have also utilized two (computationally inexpensive) approximate approaches to determine the WC-liquid phase boundary in the dual-gated system. We assess the quality of the results by comparing them to the more accurate, but much more computationally intensive, DMC results.

First, the phase transition can be approached from the crystalline side by utilizing the Lindemann melting criterion, which states that melting occurs when the fluctuations of the particles about their equilibrium lattice positions exceed a certain fraction of the lattice spacing. That is, when the parameter γ≡⟨(δ𝐫j)2/a2\gamma\equiv\sqrt{\langle{(\delta{\bf r}_{j})^{2}}/a^{2}} exceeds a critical value γc\gamma_{c}, where aa is the lattice constant. We have computed the fluctuation ⟨(δ​𝐫j)2⟩\langle{(\delta{\bf r}_{j})^{2}}\rangle in the harmonic approximation. We fix γc≈0.3\gamma_{c}\approx 0.3 by matching to the d=∞d=\infty transition (the unscreened Coulomb problem) at rs≈30r_{s}\approx 30. Details of the Lindemann-based estimate are presented in Appendix B.

Alternatively, we can approach the phase transition from the liquid side and determine the critical values of rsr_{s} via the quantum Hansen-Verlet (HV) freezing criterion [34], which states that the freezing occurs when the maximum of the liquid-state structure factor S⁡(k)S(k) attains a critical value S⁡(kmax)≈1.5S(k_{\text{max}})\approx 1.5. To obtain a suitable approximation of the structure factor of the gate-screened 2DEG, we use a variational method [35, 34]. We take as a variational wavefunction the ground state of the unscreened system with an “effective” electron charge as a variational parameter, which is then determined by minimizing the energy. The correlation functions of the unscreened system are taken from the parametrization in [36]. The specifics of the HV estimate are presented in Appendix A.

Results (double-gate). The phase diagram of the dual-gate screened 2DEG as a function of rsr_{s} and dd, obtained by DMC, is shown in Fig. 1. The locations of the WC-liquid phase boundaries obtained by the two approximate approaches are also shown for comparison, which are seen to be in qualitative agreement with DMC. We proceed by elaborating upon the DMC simulations and results, followed by a more detailed comparison to the approximate approaches.

We have analyzed the stability of the crystalline and fluid phases in the regime 20≤rs≤22020\leq r_{s}\leq 220 and d≥20d\geq 20, chosen such that the screening length and inter-electron distance are of similar magnitude. The DMC simulations are performed on a finite rsr_{s}-dd grid. The DMC phase boundary is obtained by comparing the energies of fluid and crystalline states of different spin-polarization and spin-ordering, as shown in Fig. 2 for selected values of rsr_{s} and dd. We have not tested for the possibility of any intermediate partially melted electron liquid crystalline phases [3, *Waintal2006_hybrid, 7], or partially polarized fluid phases.

As a function of gate distance dd, three main regimes are observed: (i) In the unscreened limit d→∞d\to\infty, interactions are long-range and a crystalline phase is stable for all sufficiently low densities (large rsr_{s}). When the density increases (decreasing rsr_{s}), the crystalline phase gives way to a (paramagnetic) fluid at about rs≈30r_{s}\approx 30 33 3 This value is consistent with the estimated critical rsr_{s} in 2DEG using the same method (DMC with SJB trial wave functions) [13], as expected. Recent calculations with neural quantum states indicate a value which is larger [8], but this is outside the scope of our study.. (ii) At finite dd with 30≤d<∞30\leq d<\infty, the region of stability of the Wigner crystal is bounded at both low and high density. In particular, at sufficiently low density, when the inter-electron distance is larger than the effective interaction range, a metallic state is stable. (iii) For d<30d<30, the ground state is a Fermi fluid for all simulated values of rsr_{s}. We thus identify dc≈29d_{c}\approx 29 as the critical gate distance for the existence of a WC state; for d<dcd<d_{c} the ground state is liquid for any density.

The presence of metal gates not only affects the WC-liquid transition, but also influences the spin-ordering and spin-polarization of the system. In the crystal phase, the ferromagnetic state is suppressed for stronger gate screening (smaller dd) as the interaction becomes more short-ranged. In the liquid phase, our results suggest the possibility of a region of stability for a ferromagnetic fluid for gate distances 55≲d≲6555\lesssim d\lesssim 65 as presented in Fig. 2. These results are in contrast with the case of a long-range Coulomb interaction, where no region of stability for the ferromagnetic fluid has been observed. However, we note that more careful studies are necessary to make a conclusive statement. In particular, the ferromagnetic fluid is in very close competition with the antiferromagnetic WC, with the uncertainty in the energies being of similar magnitude as the energy difference.

We probe the nature of the ground states further with the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r), which is shown in Fig. 3 for different values of rsr_{s} at a gate distance d=40d=40. Long-range oscillations are evident for Wigner crystallization at rs=60r_{s}=60, whereas they are damped in the fluid phase at rs=20r_{s}=20 and in the re-entrant fluid at rs=220r_{s}=220. While the states at rs=20r_{s}=20 and rs=220r_{s}=220 are both Fermi liquids (as further confirmed by the momentum distribution n⁡(k)n(k) in Fig. 3), subtle differences arise as a consequence of the effective interaction length ξ∝d\xi\propto d. In particular, at low rsr_{s} the effective interaction length ξ≫rs\xi\gg r_{s} and thus the shape of the correlation hole is solely determined by the inter-electron distance rsr_{s}: When plotted at given rsr_{s} for different values of gate distance dd, the short-range behavior of g↑⁣↓​(r)g_{\uparrow\downarrow}(r) does not change – see Fig. 3. On the other hand, in the re-entrant phase, where ξ<rs\xi<r_{s}, the gate distance affects the short-range behavior of g↑⁣↓​(r)g_{\uparrow\downarrow}(r). As depicted in Fig. 3, the correlation hole is more pronounced for larger gate distances dd (larger ξ\xi) if rsr_{s} is kept fixed.

The phase boundaries obtained by the Lindemann and HV criteria are in close agreement with each other and in semi-quantitative agreement with DMC (Fig. 1). In particular, the critical gate distance estimated by the approximate methods is dc≈35d_{c}\approx 35, exceeding the DMC-obtained value dc≈29d_{c}\approx 29 by only about 20%. A direct comparison of ground state energies, shown in Fig. 4, demonstrates that the qualitative dd-dependence is accurately captured by both the harmonic approximation utilized for the Lindemann criterion and the variational method used for the HV criterion. However, Fig. 4 also shows that, in contrast to DMC, the accuracy of the approximate methods is not sufficient to resolve the energy differences between different states. Nevertheless, both approximate methods offer sensible routes to estimate observables at negligible computational cost. For example, the structure factor in the fluid phase obtained by the variational method is in good agreement with DMC results (see Fig. 4). Similarly, the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r) computed in the crystalline phase via DMC and the harmonic approximation are in reasonable agreement with each other (see App. B.6).

Single-gate screening. Another common experimental setup involves a 2DEG near a single metallic gate electrode. While the dual-gate screened interaction decays exponentially at large distances, the decay is polynomial when there is only a single gate at a distance dd from the electron layer, with Vsc​(r)∼d2/r3V_{\rm sc}(r)\sim d^{2}/r^{3} for r≫dr\gg d. Given the reasonable accuracy of the Lindemann melting and HV freezing criteria in the dual-gated case, we have applied them to the single-gate geometry. The results presented in Appendix C are qualitatively similar to those in the dual-gate case, with a slight reduction in the critical gate distance, dc≈27.4d_{c}\approx 27.4 (Lindemann) and dc≈25.9d_{c}\approx 25.9 (HV), needed to completely suppress the WC.

Discussion. We have analyzed the competition between solid and liquid phases in the phase diagram of the symmetric dual-gated 2DEG using DMC methods. The WC phase forms a dome in the (rs,d)(r_{s},d) plane, consisting of a smaller dome of ferromagnetic crystal within a larger striped antiferromagnetic crystal phase. We have identified the critical gate distance for the existence of the WC as dc≈29d_{c}\approx 29. Our results suggest the possibility of a narrow region of ferromagnetic fluid at large rsr_{s} and intermediate dd. The DMC results for the phase boundary were found to be in reasonable agreement with the phase boundaries obtained by the Lindemann melting and HV freezing criteria. These melting and freezing criteria were also used to estimate the solid-liquid phase boundary in the case of a single gate electrode. Our results should be of practical importance for experimental 2DEG systems, which are often realized in gated devices.

Further investigation is required to determine whether additional intermediate phases may emerge or be stabilized by the presence of screening gates. Comparisons of the Lindemann melting and HV freezing criteria with DMC suggest that these approaches should be useful for making estimates in other experimentally realized 2DEG systems, such as those involving more complex gate geometries or dielectric environments.

Appendix A Variational calculation using the Coulomb wave-function

This calculation follows Ref. [35]. Our goal here is to test how good of a variational energy we can get for the liquid states using the variational wave-functions optimized for electrons interacting via pure Coulomb interactions for the problem of electrons interacting via screened Coulomb interactions.

More concretely, we want to find variational energies for a system with neln_{\text{el}} electrons per area interacting via two-body interaction v⁡(𝒓)v(\bm{r}). We use the variational wave function obtained for the same density of electrons interacting via vvar​(𝒓)=𝔢24​π​ϵ0​rv_{\text{var}}(\bm{r})=\frac{\mathfrak{e}^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r} and optimize over 𝔢2\mathfrak{e}^{2}, which is equivalent to optimization over 𝔯s≡m​𝔢24​π​ϵ0​π​nel\mathfrak{r}_{\text{s}}\equiv\frac{m\mathfrak{e}^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}}}.

We used the parametrization of the energy from [12] and the parametrization of the PDF from [36], which used Monte Carlo simulations for Nel=42​(45)N_{\text{el}}=42(45) electrons on a square-shaped box with periodic boundary conditions for the paramagnetic (ferromagnetic) liquid.

We find the optimal value of 𝔯s\mathfrak{r}_{\text{s}} as a function of rs=m​e24​π​ϵ0​π​nelr_{\text{s}}=\frac{me^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}}} and rd=π​nel​d2r_{\text{d}}={\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}d^{2}}}. When rdr_{\text{d}} is large, there is no screening so 𝔯s≈rs\mathfrak{r}_{\text{s}}\approx r_{\text{s}}. However, when rdr_{\text{d}} is small the screening is effective so 𝔯s≪rs\mathfrak{r}_{\text{s}}\ll r_{\text{s}}. In Fig. 5, we show a plot of 𝔯s\mathfrak{r}_{\text{s}} versus rsr_{\text{s}} for various values of d=rs​rdd={r_{\text{s}}}{r_{\text{d}}} and for the double gate cases.

Appendix B Semi-classical approximation for Wigner crystal

The semiclassical approximation for the Wigner crystal is not variational. For the Coulomb WC, this approximation works well up to rs≈30r_{\text{s}}\approx 30. For instance, the energy and pair distribution functions match semi-quantitatively with Monte Carlo calculations.

We modify the classical calculation Ref. [37] for the Coulomb potentials screened by two gates at a distance dd from the 2DEG.

B.1 Minimization of classical energy

Deep in the Wigner crystal phase, the electrons minimize the interaction energy by staying as far as possible from each other. We assume that this achieved by localizing the electrons in a Bravais lattice, Λ\Lambda.

The classical energy per electron can be written as

EClNel=12∑𝑹∈Λ:𝑹≠𝟎V(|𝑹|).\frac{E_{\rm Cl}}{N_{\text{el}}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bm{R}}\in\Lambda:{\bm{R}}\neq{\bm{0}}}V(|{\bm{R}}|). (4)

In terms of the basis vectors 𝒂1{\bm{a}}_{1} and 𝒂2{\bm{a}}_{2}, we can write 𝑹=n1​𝒂1+n2​𝒂2{\bm{R}}=n_{1}{\bm{a}}_{1}+n_{2}{\bm{a}}_{2} with n1,n2∈ℤn_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}, then the lattice is specified by the inner products gi​j≡⟨𝒂i|𝒂j⟩g_{ij}\equiv\langle{\bm{a}}_{i}|{\bm{a}}_{j}\rangle. The unit cell size is specified by |det(g)|\sqrt{|\det(g)|} and it is equal to 1/nel1/n_{\text{el}}.

We now restrict to the case of interactions of the form

V⁡(r)=∫0∞e−t​r2​Φ​(t)​𝑑tV(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm e}^{-tr^{2}}\Phi(t)\mathrm{d}{t} (5)

with Φ⁡(t)≥0\Phi(t)\geq 0. The potential VscV_{\rm{sc}} of Eq. 3 is of this form with Φ(t)=1π​t∑n∈ℤ(−1)ne−4​n2​d2​t=1π​tθ4(e−4​d2​t)=12​d​tθ2(e−π2/(4d2t))\Phi(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(-1)^{n}{\rm e}^{-4n^{2}d^{2}t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\theta_{4}(e^{-4d^{2}t})=\frac{1}{2dt}\theta_{2}(e^{-\pi^{2}/(4d^{2}t)}). Here θ2\theta_{2} and θ4\theta_{4} are Jacobi Theta functions.

The classical energy can then be written as

EClNel=12​∫0∞[ϑΛ​(t)−1]​Φ​(t)​𝑑t\frac{E_{\rm Cl}}{N_{\text{el}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left[\vartheta_{\Lambda}(t)-1\right]\Phi(t)\mathrm{d}{t} (6)

with

ϑΛ​(t)=∑𝑹∈Λe−t​|𝑹|2=∑𝒎∈ℤ2e−t​b​(𝒎);b⁡([m1,m2])=m12​g11+2​g12​m1​m2+m22​g22.\begin{split}\vartheta_{\Lambda}(t)&=\sum_{{\bm{R}}\in\Lambda}{\rm e}^{-t|{\bm{R}}|^{2}}=\sum_{{\bm{m}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}{\rm e}^{-tb({\bm{m}})};\\ b([m_{1},m_{2}])&=m_{1}^{2}g_{11}+2g_{12}m_{1}m_{2}+m_{2}^{2}g_{22}.\end{split} (7)

B.2 Separation of scales

For various calculations, it is convenient to split the potential into a long-ranged piece and a short-ranged piece.

For the potentials of the form in Eq. 5, this can be achieved in terms of a length scale t0\sqrt{t_{0}}:

VLR​(r,t0)≡∫0t0e−t​r2​Φ​(t)​𝑑t;\displaystyle V_{\rm{LR}}(r;t_{0})\equiv\int_{0}^{t_{0}}{\rm e}^{-tr^{2}}\Phi(t)\mathrm{d}{t}; (8)
VSR​(r,t0)≡∫t0∞e−t​r2​Φ​(t)​𝑑t.\displaystyle V_{\rm{SR}}(r;t_{0})\equiv\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}{\rm e}^{-tr^{2}}\Phi(t)\mathrm{d}{t}. (9)

LR and SR stand for long-ranged and short-ranged, respectively. One can see that the LR and SR become short-ranged and long-ranged, respectively, in momentum space:

V~LR​(q,t0)=∫0t0e−q24​t​π​Φ​(t)t​𝑑t;\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\rm{LR}}(q;t_{0})=\int_{0}^{t_{0}}{\rm e}^{-\frac{q^{2}}{4t}}\frac{\pi\Phi(t)}{t}\mathrm{d}{t}; (10)
V~SR​(q,t0)=∫t0∞e−q24​t​π​Φ​(t)t​𝑑t.\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\rm{SR}}(q;t_{0})=\int_{t_{0}}^{\infty}{\rm e}^{-\frac{q^{2}}{4t}}\frac{\pi\Phi(t)}{t}\mathrm{d}{t}. (11)

where V~β​(q,t0)=2​π​∫0∞J0​(q​r)​Vβ​(r,t0)​r​𝑑r\tilde{V}_{\rm\beta}(q;t_{0})=2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{0}(qr)V_{\beta}(r;t_{0})r\mathrm{d}{r} with β=SR,LR\beta={\rm SR,LR} and J0J_{0} is the zeroth-order Bessel function.

For the Coulomb potential, it is convenient to choose t0=π​nelt_{0}=\pi n_{\text{el}}. In this case

VSR​(r,π​nel)\displaystyle V_{\rm SR}(r;\pi n_{\text{el}}) =erfc⁡(π​nel​r2)r\displaystyle=\frac{\erfc(\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}r^{2}})}{r} (12)
VLR​(r,π​nel)\displaystyle V_{\rm LR}(r;\pi n_{\text{el}}) =erf⁡(π​nel​r2)r\displaystyle=\frac{\erf(\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}r^{2}})}{r} (13)
V~SR​(q,π​nel)\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\rm SR}(q;\pi n_{\text{el}}) =2​π​erf⁡(q2/(4​π​nel))q\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi\erf(\sqrt{q^{2}/(4\pi n_{\text{el}})})}{q} (14)
V~LR​(q,π​nel)\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\rm LR}(q;\pi n_{\text{el}}) =2​π​erfc⁡(q2/(4​π​nel))q\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi\erfc(\sqrt{q^{2}/(4\pi n_{\text{el}})})}{q} (15)

For the double gated potential and poor screening (π​nel​d2≳1\pi n_{\text{el}}d^{2}\gtrsim 1), it is convenient to split

VSR​(r)=1r​erfc⁡(π​nel​r2),V~LR​(q)=2​πq​(erfc⁡(q2/(4​π​nel))−2e2​q​d+1).\begin{split}{V}_{\rm SR}(r)&=\frac{1}{r}\erfc(\sqrt{\pi n_{\text{el}}r^{2}}),\\ \tilde{V}_{\rm LR}(q)&=\frac{2\pi}{q}\left(\erfc(\sqrt{q^{2}/(4\pi n_{\text{el}})})-\frac{2}{e^{2qd}+1}\right).\end{split} (16)

In other words, we use separation of scales for the direct piece of the interactions. The sums over the interaction with the image charges is done in momentum space because 2/(e2​q​d+1)2/(e^{2qd}+1) decays exponentially.

When screening is good (π​nel​d2≲1\pi n_{\text{el}}d^{2}\lesssim 1), we evaluated the sums directly in real space because the potential decays exponentially as e−πr/2de^{-\pi r/2d}. To be more precise, we use the expression Vsc​(r)=e24​π​ϵ0​r​υ​(π​r2​d)V_{\rm{sc}}(r)=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r}\upsilon(\tfrac{\pi r}{2d}), where

υ⁡(x)=∫0∞2π​xsinh⁡(cosh⁡(s)​x)​𝑑s.\upsilon(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{x}{\sinh(\cosh(s)x)}\mathrm{d}{s}. (17)

The latter expression for VscV_{\rm{sc}} is obtained by combining Eq. B7 of Ref. [15] with the integral representation for the modified Bessel function K0​(x)=∫0∞e−x​cosh⁡(s)​𝑑sK_{0}(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x\cosh(s)}ds.

B.3 Evaluation of the classical energy

To compare the energy of the crystal with the energy of the fluid, it is convenient to split the uniform component of the energy.

2​EClNel\displaystyle\frac{2E_{\rm Cl}}{N_{\text{el}}} =nel​V~​(0)+USR+ULR;\displaystyle=n_{\text{el}}\tilde{V}(0)+U_{\rm SR}+U_{\rm LR}; (18)
USR\displaystyle U_{\rm SR} =−VLR​(0)+∑𝑹∈Λ′VSR​(|𝑹|);\displaystyle=-V_{\rm LR}(0)+\sum_{{\bm{R}}\in\Lambda}^{\prime}V_{\rm SR}(|{\bm{R}}|); (19)
ULRnel\displaystyle\frac{U_{\rm LR}}{n_{\text{el}}} =−V~SR​(0)+∑𝑮∈Λ∨′V~LR​(|𝑮|),\displaystyle=-\tilde{V}_{\rm SR}(0)+\sum_{{\bm{G}}\in\Lambda^{\vee}}^{\prime}\tilde{V}_{\rm LR}(|{\bm{G}}|), (20)

where Λ∨\Lambda^{\vee} is the dual lattice and the primed sums mean to omit the zero vector. The first term in Eq. 18 is canceled by the neutralizing background. We thus identify the classical energy per electron for the crystal phase in the presence of a neutralizing background as

δ​ECl≡USR+ULR2.\delta E_{\rm Cl}\equiv\frac{U_{\rm SR}+U_{\rm LR}}{2}. (21)

In Fig. 6, we show δ​ECl\delta E_{\rm Cl} for the double-gate potential as a function of rd≡π​n​d2=d/rsr_{\text{d}}\equiv\sqrt{\pi nd^{2}}=d/r_{\text{s}}. The answer for the Coulomb case is C0∗/a0C_{0}^{*}/a_{0} with C0∗≈−2.10671C_{0}^{*}\approx-2.10671 and a0a_{0} the WC lattice constant, or equivalently the Madelung constant C0≈−1.1061C_{0}\approx-1.1061. We obtained the asymptotic behavior as follows. For the large rdr_{\text{d}}, we use the separation of scales in Eq. 16. Then the difference of δ​ECl\delta E_{\rm Cl} with respect to the pure Coulomb case, comes from the terms involving VLRV_{\rm LR}. The change from −VLR​(0)-V_{\rm LR}(0) is

∫0∞2​πq​2e2​q​d+1​q​d​q2​π=log⁡(2)/d\int_{0}^{\infty}\,\frac{2\pi}{q}\frac{2}{e^{2qd}+1}\frac{q\mathrm{d}{q}}{2\pi}=\log(2)/d (22)

The other corrections come from the sum at finite momenta in ULRU_{\rm LR}. All these contributions are suppressed by exp⁡(−2​|𝑮|​d)\exp(-2|{{\bm{G}}}|d):

rs∗δ​ECl=C0+log⁡(2)2​rd−1π​∑𝑮∈Λ×∨2​πrs​G​11+e2​rd​(rs​G)r_{\text{s}}*\delta E_{\rm Cl}=C_{0}+\frac{\log(2)}{2r_{\text{d}}}-\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{{\bm{G}}\in\Lambda^{\vee}_{\times}}\frac{2\pi}{r_{\text{s}}G}\frac{1}{1+e^{2r_{\text{d}}(r_{\text{s}}G)}} (23)

For small rdr_{\text{d}} the interactions decay exponentially, so that to exponential order δ​ECl\delta E_{\rm Cl} is −nelv~(𝟎)/2=−πneld=−rd/rs-n_{\text{el}}\tilde{v}({\bm{0}})/2=-\pi n_{\text{el}}d=-r_{\text{d}}/r_{\text{s}}. We get

rs∗δ​ECl=−rd+∑𝑹∈Λ×υ⁡(π2​rd​Rrs)2​R/rsr_{\text{s}}*\delta E_{\rm Cl}=-r_{\text{d}}+\sum_{{\bm{R}}\in\Lambda_{\times}}\frac{\upsilon(\tfrac{\pi}{2r_{\text{d}}}\tfrac{R}{r_{\text{s}}})}{2R/r_{\text{s}}} (24)

B.4 Phonon spectrum

Now that we have minimized the potential energy, we need to minimize the kinetic energy. To do so, we let the electrons deviate from their equilibrium positions. These oscillations impose a restoring force on the electrons that is of the order ∂Ra∂RbV⁡(R)\partial_{R_{a}}\partial_{R_{b}}V(R). The balance between the restoring force and the kinetic energy gives rise to the collective phonon modes of the Wigner crystal.

We assume that electrons are well-localized near the sites of the triangular lattice so that we can treat them as distinguishable particles. In the harmonic approximation, we obtain

HHar=∑j𝒑j22​m+∑i,jδ​𝒓i​Ki​j​δ​𝒓j2H_{\rm Har}=\sum_{j}\frac{{\bm{p}}^{2}_{j}}{2m}+\sum_{i,j}\frac{\delta\bm{r}_{i}K_{ij}\delta\bm{r}_{j}}{2} (25)

where δ​𝒓j=𝒓j−𝑹j\delta\bm{r}_{j}=\bm{r}_{j}-{\bm{R}}_{j} is the position of the jj-th electron relative to its equilibrium position, 𝑹j{\bm{R}}_{j}. The elastic matrix is

[Ki​i]a​b=∑𝑹∂2V⁡(R)∂Ra​∂Rb′;[Ki​j]a​b=−∂2V⁡(R=|𝑹i​j|)∂Ra​∂Rb(j≠i).\begin{split}[K_{ii}]_{ab}&=\sum_{{\bm{R}}}{{}^{\prime}}\frac{\partial^{2}V(R)}{\partial R_{a}\partial R_{b}};\\ [K_{ij}]_{ab}&=-\frac{\partial^{2}V(R=|{\bm{R}}_{ij}|)}{\partial R_{a}\partial R_{b}}\quad(j\neq i).\end{split} (26)

The Hamiltonian HHarH_{\rm Har} is diagonalized through a Fourier transform: 𝒑~𝒒=1Nel​∑je−i​𝒒​𝑹j​𝒑j\tilde{{\bm{p}}}_{{\bm{q}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{el}}}\sum_{j}{\rm e}^{-{\rm i}{\bm{q}}{\bm{R}}_{j}}{\bm{p}}_{j}, δ​𝒓~𝒒=1Nel​∑jei​𝒒​𝑹j​δ​𝒓j\delta\tilde{\bm{r}}_{{\bm{q}}}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{el}}}\sum_{j}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}{\bm{q}}{\bm{R}}_{j}}\delta\bm{r}_{j} and

K~(𝒒)=∑j≠0ei​𝒒​𝑹jK0​j=∑𝑹(1−cos(𝒒𝑹))′κ(𝑹),\tilde{K}({\bm{q}})=\sum_{j\neq 0}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}{\bm{q}}{\bm{R}}_{j}}K_{0j}=\sum_{{\bm{R}}}{{}^{\prime}}(1-\cos({\bm{q}}{\bm{R}}))\kappa({\bm{R}}), (27)

with

κ​(𝑹)a​b=𝒟⟂​(δa​b−R^a​R^b)+𝒟∥​R^a​R^bR3,\kappa({\bm{R}})_{ab}=\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\perp}(\delta_{ab}-\hat{R}_{a}\hat{R}_{b})+\mathcal{D}_{\parallel}\hat{R}_{a}\hat{R}_{b}}{R^{3}}, (28)

where 𝒟⟂\mathcal{D}_{\perp} and 𝒟⟂\mathcal{D}_{\perp} are functions of the ratio |𝑹|/d|{\bm{R}}|/d.

The dynamical matrix is then D​(𝒒)=K~​(𝒒)/mD({\bm{q}})=\tilde{K}({\bm{q}})/m so that the phonon frequencies ωk​(𝒒)\omega_{k}({\bm{q}}) are the (non-negative) square roots of the eigenvalues of D⁡(𝒒)D({\bm{q}}), and k=1,2k=1,2 label the two phonon branches. Recall that D⁡(𝒒)=(1/rs3)​K¯​(𝒒)D({\bm{q}})=(1/r_{\text{s}}^{3})\bar{K}({\bm{q}}).

The semi-classical energy is then

ESemiClNel=∫𝒒ω1​(𝒒)+ω2​(𝒒)2.\frac{E_{\rm SemiCl}}{N_{\text{el}}}=\int_{{\bm{q}}}\frac{\omega_{1}({\bm{q}})+\omega_{2}({\bm{q}})}{2}. (29)

where the integral ∫𝒒\int_{{\bm{q}}} is over the Brillouin zone of the WC and normalized to ∫𝒒1=1\int_{{\bm{q}}}1=1 44 4 In practice, we approximate ∫𝒒\int_{{\bm{q}}} by a finite sum over a uniform grid of the Wigner crystal’ Brillouin zone: ∫𝒒=14​N1​N2∑𝒒\int_{{\bm{q}}}=\frac{1}{4N_{1}N_{2}}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}, with 𝒒=j1N1​𝑮1+j2N2​𝑮2{\bm{q}}=\frac{j_{1}}{N_{1}}{\bm{G}}_{1}+\frac{j_{2}}{N_{2}}{\bm{G}}_{2} with −Na<ja≤Na​(a=1,2)-N_{a}<j_{a}\leq N_{a}\,(a=1,2). When calculating the Lindemann parameter we simply omit the 𝒒=𝟎{\bm{q}}={\bm{0}}..

B.5 Melting of Wigner crystal

We estimate the location of the melting instability through the Lindemann criterion. First, we calculate the Lindemann parameter γ≡⟨δ​𝒓02⟩/a2\gamma\equiv\sqrt{{\langle\delta\bm{r}^{2}_{0}\rangle}/{a^{2}}}, where aa is the Wigner crystal lattice constant which is given by a=(43)1/4/nela=\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{1/4}/\sqrt{n_{\text{el}}} for the triangular lattice. The expectation value should be calculated with the ground state of the (full) phonon Hamiltonian. However, we will use the ground state of the harmonic Hamiltonian, HHarH_{\rm Har}.

We can evaluate γ\gamma in terms of the phonon spectrum:

γ2=1a2​∫𝒒∑k12​m​ωk​(𝒒).\gamma^{2}=\frac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{{\bm{q}}}\sum_{k}\frac{1}{2m\omega_{k}({\bm{q}})}\,. (30)

For potentials of the form v⁡(r)=e24​π​ϵ​r​u​(r/d)v(r)=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon r}u(r/d) for some function uu, we can write ωk​(𝒒)=1m​a3​aB​ω¯k​(𝒒​a,d/a)\omega_{k}({\bm{q}})=\frac{1}{m\sqrt{a^{3}a_{\text{B}}}}\bar{\omega}_{k}({\bm{q}}a;d/a), with ω¯\bar{\omega} dimensionless frequencies that only depend on the shown variables. From this follows that

γ2=Υ⁡(d/a)rs,Υ=𝒩​∫𝒒∑k1ω¯k​(𝒒),\gamma^{2}=\frac{\Upsilon(d/a)}{\sqrt{r_{\text{s}}}},\quad\Upsilon=\mathcal{N}\int_{{\bm{q}}}\sum_{k}\frac{1}{\bar{\omega}_{k}({\bm{q}})}, (31)

with 𝒩=332​π4≈0.362297\mathcal{N}=\sqrt[4]{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{32\pi}}\approx 0.362297 and k=1,2k=1,2 refers to the two phonon bands.

Deep in the WC phase, γ≪1\gamma\ll 1. The transition occurs at some critical value γc\gamma_{c}. This value seems to be ‘universal’ [34]. In practice, we determine γc\gamma_{c} by calculating γ\gamma at a point in parameter space we believe the melting transition occurs. From the scaling of the γ\gamma in Eq. 31, we find the following scaling for the critical rsr_{\text{s}} at gate distance dd, rs⋆​(d)r_{\text{s}}^{\star}(d):

rs⋆​(d1)rs⋆​(d2)=(Υ⁡(d1/a)Υ⁡(d2/a))2.\frac{r_{\text{s}}^{\star}(d_{1})}{r_{\text{s}}^{\star}(d_{2})}=\left(\frac{\Upsilon(d_{1}/a)}{\Upsilon(d_{2}/a)}\right)^{2}. (32)

In the main text, we used that rs⋆​(∞)=30.1r_{\text{s}}^{\star}(\infty)=30.1, which is extracted from the transition between the WC and fluid phases.

B.6 Pair distribution function

We calculate the pair distribution function (PDF) from the phonon spectrum to compare with the Monte Carlo results.

The PDF is defined to be

nel2​g​(𝒓):=nelNel​∑i≠j⟨δ⁡(𝒓−𝒓i+𝒓j)⟩,n_{\text{el}}^{2}g(\bm{r}):=\frac{n_{\text{el}}}{N_{\text{el}}}\sum_{i\neq j}\langle{\delta(\bm{r}-\bm{r}_{i}+\bm{r}_{j})}\rangle, (33)

where the sum is over electrons, neln_{\text{el}} is the electron density, NelN_{\text{el}} is the number of electrons and 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} is the position of the electron localized near 𝑹i{\bm{R}}_{i}. The expectation value is taken with respect to the ground state of the harmonic Hamiltonian.

Using the integral representation of the two-dimensional delta function, we obtain

g⁡(𝒓)=1Nel​nel​∑i≠j∫d2​𝒒(2​π)2​⟨exp⁡(i​𝒒⋅(𝒓−𝒓i​j))⟩;=1Nel​nel​∑i≠j∫d2​𝒒(2​π)2​ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓−𝑹i​j)​e−⟨(𝒒⋅(𝒓i​j−𝑹i​j))2⟩2;\begin{split}g(\bm{r})&=\frac{1}{N_{\text{el}}n_{\text{el}}}\sum_{i\neq j}\int\!\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}{{\bm{q}}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\langle{\exp({\rm i}{\bm{q}}\cdot(\bm{r}-\bm{r}_{ij}))}\rangle;\\ &=\frac{1}{N_{\text{el}}n_{\text{el}}}\sum_{i\neq j}\int\!\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}{{\bm{q}}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}{\bm{q}}\cdot(\bm{r}-{\bm{R}}_{ij})}{\rm e}^{-\frac{\langle{({\bm{q}}\cdot(\bm{r}_{ij}-{\bm{R}}_{ij}))^{2}}\rangle}{2}};\end{split} (34)

here 𝒓i​j:=𝒓i−𝒓j\bm{r}_{ij}:=\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j} and 𝑹i​j:=𝑹i−𝑹j{\bm{R}}_{ij}:={\bm{R}}_{i}-{\bm{R}}_{j}.

The expectation value in the exponent can be expressed in terms of the harmonic spectrum as

[𝒢i​j]a​b:=⟨[𝒓i​j−𝑹i​j]a​[𝒓i​j−𝑹i​j]b⟩=1Nel​∑𝐤,λ1−cos⁡(𝐤⋅𝑹i​j)m​ωλ​(𝐤)​[e𝐤,λ]a​[e𝐤,λ]b,\begin{split}\left[\mathcal{G}_{ij}\right]_{ab}&:=\langle[\bm{r}_{ij}-{\bm{R}}_{ij}]_{a}[\bm{r}_{ij}-{\bm{R}}_{ij}]_{b}\rangle\\ &=\frac{1}{N_{\text{el}}}\sum_{{\bf{k}},\lambda}\frac{1-\cos({\bf{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}_{ij})}{m\omega_{\lambda}({\bf{k}})}[e_{{\bf{k}},\lambda}]_{a}[e_{{\bf{k}},\lambda}]_{b},\end{split} (35)

where e𝐤,λe_{{\bf{k}},\lambda} is a real vector satisfying K~​(𝐤)​e𝐤,λ=m​[ωλ​(𝐤)]2​e𝐤,λ\tilde{K}({\bf{k}})e_{{\bf{k}},\lambda}=m[\omega_{\lambda}({\bf{k}})]^{2}e_{{\bf{k}},\lambda}. When |𝑹i​j|→∞|{\bm{R}}_{ij}|\to\infty, 𝒢i​j∼δa​b​⟨(𝒓0−𝑹0)​2⟩\mathcal{G}_{ij}\sim\delta_{ab}\langle{(\bm{r}_{0}-{\bm{R}}_{0})2}\rangle.

From lattice translation invariance, we find

g⁡(𝒓)=1nel∑j≠0∫d2​𝒒(2​π)2ei​𝒒​(𝒓−𝑹j​0)exp(−𝒒⋅𝒢j​0⋅𝒒/2);=1nel​∑j≠0exp(−(𝒓−𝑹j​0)⋅𝒢j​0−1⋅(𝒓−𝑹j​0)/2)2​π​det(𝒢j​0).\begin{split}g(\bm{r})&=\frac{1}{n_{\text{el}}}\sum_{j\neq 0}\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}{{\bm{q}}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}{\rm e}^{{\rm i}{\bm{q}}(\bm{r}-{\bm{R}}_{j0})}\exp(-{\bm{q}}\cdot\mathcal{G}_{j0}\cdot{\bm{q}}/2);\\ &=\frac{1}{n_{\text{el}}}\sum_{j\neq 0}\frac{\exp(-(\bm{r}-{\bm{R}}_{j0})\cdot\mathcal{G}_{j0}^{-1}\cdot(\bm{r}-{\bm{R}}_{j0})/2)}{2\pi\sqrt{\det(\mathcal{G}_{j0})}}.\end{split} (36)

The radial pair distribution function (rPDF) is defined as

g¯​(r):=∫d​θ2​π​g​(𝒓)=12​π​r​1nel​Nel​∑i≠j⟨δ⁡(r−ri​j)⟩,\begin{split}\bar{g}(r)&:=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}{\theta}}{2\pi}g(\bm{r})=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\frac{1}{n_{\text{el}}N_{\text{el}}}\sum_{i\neq j}\langle\delta(r-r_{ij})\rangle,\end{split} (37)

where ri​j:=|𝒓i−𝒓j|r_{ij}:=|\bm{r}_{i}-{\bm{r}}_{j}|. We find g¯​(r)\bar{g}(r) by numerically integrating g⁡(𝒓)g(\bm{r}) in Eq. 36.

Appendix C Single gate potential

In the presence of a single gate at a distance dd, Vsc​(r)=e24​π​ϵ​(1r−1r2+4​d2)V_{\rm{sc}}(r)=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{r^{2}+4d^{2}}}\right). We show the phase diagram in Fig. 8 using the freezing approximation (V.H. criteria) and the melting approximation (Lindemann criteria). The approximations do not explicitly account for the magnetic order. However, we anticipate that the Wigner crystal is a striped anti-ferromagnet, while the Fermi fluid is likely unpolarized, as in the double-gated two-dimensional electron gas.

The evaluation of the VH criteria is straightforward. To calculate the Lindemann parameter, we followed the same steps as in Appendices B.4 and  B.5. The main difference is that in the good screening regime, the evaluation in real space is somewhat slow. We instead used the separation of scales (Ewald method) as we did for the pure Coulomb interaction with Φ⁡(t)=1−exp⁡(−4​d2​t)π​t\Phi(t)=\frac{1-\exp(-4d^{2}t)}{\sqrt{\pi t}}.
